messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marianne is a 50-year-old jeweler who has lived alone for years and once took pride in how steady her hands were, how easily she could spend a day bent over a workbench setting stones under a bright lamp. The assault happened eight months ago after she closed her small studio one winter evening. She had stayed late finishing a repair, and when she stepped into the alley behind the building a man she had noticed earlier in the day approached her, first asking for the time and then moving in close before she could get back inside. What stays with her is not a complete sequence but shards: the smell of his jacket, the flash of his face near hers, the force of being pinned, the instant she realized no one was coming. Other stretches are simply gone. She says some moments are “photographic” and others disappear entirely, and when more of it starts to come she cuts it off almost automatically, as if finishing the memory would make it happen again.

Since then the memory has not behaved like a story she can tell from beginning to end. Pieces arrive without warning and vanish just as fast: his cheek in profile, the sound of his breathing, the sightline toward the metal door she could not reach. Because those pieces kept breaking into the present, she began to find bits of the assault everywhere around her: a man turning his head at the same angle, the rasp of someone breathing too near the counter, the look of dusk on the alley behind the studio all started to register as charged warnings before she could talk herself out of them. Those fragments make certain moments in the present feel charged before she has time to think. If a customer in the shop has a similar build or angle of movement, she feels she has seen the offender again. At other times it is less visual than bodily; nausea rises abruptly in her throat and stomach, and she knows something in her has been pulled toward the assault even if she cannot yet say what. News stories or casual conversations about people losing loved ones can catch her off guard too, stirring the same sense of dread and helplessness that clings to the blank spaces in her memory.

These triggers now organize how Marianne moves through the world. In her studio, where strangers regularly come in with repairs, she watches the door constantly and maps the path to the back exit the moment anyone enters. If a man steps too close to the counter, or if nausea hits while she is alone in the shop, her body reacts as though ordinary contact is dangerous. She has become convinced that strangers approaching her, even politely, may suddenly turn threatening. Restaurants, supply stores, even the lobby of her apartment building are assessed first for escape routes, and she feels truly safe only at home, in one chair by the window with the deadbolt checked. The more she lives this way, the more quickly her attention catches on possible signs of the offender in other people—an expression, a coat, a certain way of standing—so that the range of things that set her off has gradually widened.

What frightens Marianne almost as much as the assault itself is what she has come to believe her reactions say about her. When a customer’s build or a passing mention of death set her off, the trigger itself seemed to tell her something damning and final—that she was now the kind of person who could be undone by ordinary moments, and that the assault had left her permanently damaged. When she doubles over with nausea after hearing someone mention a death, or freezes because a customer resembles the man in the alley, she tells herself this proves she is “a lousy coper.” She used to think of herself as practical and self-contained; now she sees herself as weak, overreactive, and permanently altered. She also describes feeling dirty in a way she cannot wash off. On some mornings she showers before opening the studio and still feels contaminated, as if the assault left something on her. Those moments are followed by a deadened, hollow state she calls feeling “dead inside.” Because she reads the triggers as evidence of damage and contamination, each new reaction confirms for her that the world is not only unsafe but that she is especially unprotected in it.

That belief has sharpened her sense of danger. Marianne enters every room already braced, scanning exits before she notices décor or faces, and she sits where no one can come up behind her. Living at that pitch of alertness seems to make the world generate more reminders: once she is already on guard, almost any unfamiliar movement in the shop or sound in the apartment lobby can tip instantly into something her body reads as a sign of the alley. Being on guard so constantly seems to keep the assault close to the surface. In the middle of helping a client choose a setting, she can suddenly be hit by a vivid scrap of the alley and then push it away before it develops further. She is certain that if she lets the memory fill in, she will lose control; yet because she never reaches the end of it, it returns in disconnected bursts. Over months she has cut back her hours, avoids being alone in the studio near closing time, and has lost regular customers because she rushes interactions or cancels appointments.

Marianne finally sought help after a man came into the shop last week just before dusk, and the combination of his approach, the nausea that surged up, and the immediate search for the exit left her unable to speak to him. After he left, she locked the door early and sat at her bench feeling blank and ashamed. She says she is afraid that her life is shrinking to a few “safe zones” and that she will soon be unable to work at all. At the same time, she is hoping there may be a way to remember what happened without being overwhelmed by it, and to stop feeling that the assault is still waiting for her in every stranger who walks through the door.
